nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p3.translation: Foreword The curricula and guidelines form the basis for the school's mission to successfully enable students to participate and to shape their future independently. Societal and technological change as well as the further development of subjects require that educational goals and content be repeatedly formulated in a contemporary manner. About ten years after the last curriculum revision, new versions of the core curricula for lower secondary education at the Gymnasium are now available on the occasion of the introduction of the new G9. They take into account the new regulation of the duration of the educational pathway at the Gymnasium and form the curricular foundation for a progressive Gymnasium education. At the Gymnasium, subject matter expertise and scientific propaedeutics have a special status. The new core curricula strengthen and sharpen this Gymnasium educational mandate by specifying obligatory knowledge, skills, and abilities more concretely and clearly than before. With regard to education in an increasingly digital world, the core curricula of all subjects therefore also professionally incorporate the goals of the NRW media competence framework. With these core curricula and the NRW media competence framework, a binding foundation has thus been created to make learning and living with digital media a matter of course in the teaching of all subjects, and for all subjects to contribute their specific part to the development of the required competencies. Core curricula set statewide standards. They focus on the learning outcomes expected from students in the educational pathway, encompassing both knowledge and skills. The determination of ways to achieve these is left to the responsible persons on site by the core curricula. At the school level, the curricular requirements must be specified in school-internal curricula. In these, the requirements of the core curriculum intertwine with the concrete framework conditions of the school, the L

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p7.translation: 7 Preliminary remarks: Core curricula as competence-oriented teaching guidelines Core curricula make an important contribution to securing the level of demand at the individual school as well as throughout the state and create necessary prerequisites for the comparability of learning outcomes. Core curricula • provide all those involved in the school with orientation regarding the tasks and objectives of the subjects, • specify a curricular gradation and determine which subject-related competences including underlying knowledge bases students should have acquired by the end of the stages, • represent a statewide obligation structured into subject-specific content and related subject competences, • form the basis for the review of learning outcomes and performance levels, • focus on verifiable subject knowledge and skills. Statements on general, cross-subject relevant educational and upbringing goals are essentially made outside the core curricula, among others in guidelines and framework specifications. They are to be taken into account alongside the subject-specific requirements of the core curricula when developing school-specific guidelines and designing instruction. • form the curricular basis for the development of school-specific teaching guidelines or internal school curricula (§ 29 as well as § 70 School Act NRW). Since core curricula are limited to central subject skills and knowledge bases, schools are given the opportunity but also the task to design given freedoms according to school and learning group. In connection with the school program, priorities are set in instruction in terms of content, didactics, and methodology.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p8.translation: 8 1 Tasks and Objectives of the Subject Mathematics is one of the most significant global cultural achievements, which has developed over thousands of years in the search for the key to understanding the world. It represents an independent structure of concepts, theories, and structures that makes it possible to capture and understand segments of natural reality and processes in complex systems such as the economy and society. As the language of the natural sciences and technology, mathematics enables scientific developments and solutions to technical problems and thus makes a significant contribution to shaping our modern world. Likewise, insights gained with mathematical methods in politics and economics as well as in the social and humanities sciences often form the basis for decisions. The goal of mathematics instruction is the deepened mathematical basic education of the students. Deepened mathematical basic education is the ability to recognize the role that mathematics plays in the world, to make well-founded mathematical judgments, and to be prepared for present and future societal and individual demands. This core curriculum implements the KMK educational standards and is oriented towards the concept of a general education mathematics instruction 1. Accordingly, the following fundamental experiences should be made possible for students in mathematics instruction with the goal of mathematical basic education in particular: • to perceive, understand, assess, and influence technical, natural, social, and cultural phenomena and processes with the help of mathematics (mathematics as application), • to recognize and further develop mathematical objects and facts, represented in language, symbols, and images, as intellectual creations, as a deductively ordered world of their own kind (mathematics as structure), • in the engagement with m

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p9.translation: 9 in the digital world, in economy and politics, and in everyday social life. As a basis for objective assessments of data and information, the advanced mathematical basic education to be achieved enables well-founded arguments in decision-making processes and thus contributes to the development of a sense of responsibility and to the development of personality. Through central ideas and fundamental elementary mathematical concepts, the significance of mathematics as a cultural achievement is made exemplarily tangible in mathematics lessons. Understanding mathematics as a global cultural asset contributes, just like languages and literature, to the foundation of cultural coherence. In mathematics lessons, individual approaches or creative solutions are developed, exchanged, and discussed when solving tasks and dealing with problems. Even when taking detours or wrong paths, new insights are gained through reflection. The impact of mathematics lessons unfolds both in the individual engagement with subject structures and in mutual understanding and cooperation. Mathematics lessons designed in this way contribute significantly to the advanced general education of students and have an effect far beyond the school years. The deliberate, systematic approach, precise use of language, and logically correct argumentation when grasping connections develop the thinking and abstraction abilities of students. When discovering connections and regularities, as well as comparing and evaluating solution methods, cognitive strategies are formed. As a result, students are able to perceive situations from different perspectives and vary questions. The systematic analysis of questions typical for mathematics makes it possible to form a well-founded personal opinion. The students gel

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p10.translation: 10 is enabled through diverse and varying forms of instruction, ranging from understanding-oriented knowledge transfer by the teacher to discovery-based learning. Learning from errors is an inherent part of the learning process. In such designed mathematics instruction, the discussion about the validity and transferability of procedures and models is a source of new insights. Mathematics instruction must encourage girls as well as boys to confidently pursue their interest in mathematical contexts and thus utilize their abilities and developmental potentials. It should also demonstrate that mathematical knowledge opens up attractive professional perspectives for both women and men. According to the educational mandate of the Gymnasium, the subject of mathematics contributes to providing students with a deepened general education and enables them, according to their achievements and inclinations, to continue their educational path at a university or in vocationally qualifying educational programs in accordance with the qualifications in upper secondary education (Sekundarstufe II). Within the framework of the general educational and upbringing mandate of the school, instruction in mathematics supports the development of a mature and socially responsible personality and makes further contributions to interdisciplinary cross-sectional tasks in school and instruction, including among others: • human rights education, • values education, • political education and democracy education, • education for the digital world and media education, • education for sustainable development, • gender-sensitive education, • cultural and intercultural education. Language is a necessary tool in the development of competencies and therefore has a special significance for the acquisition of mathematical basic education. Cognitive processes of mathematical arguing, communicating, modeling, problem solving and

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p11.translation: 11 The interdisciplinary linking of steps in cumulative competence development, content-related cooperation with other subjects and learning areas, as well as extracurricular learning and cooperation with extracurricular partners can contribute both to achieving and deepening the respective subject-specific goals and to fulfilling overarching tasks. The present core curriculum is designed in such a way that it allows room for deepening, school-specific projects, and current developments. The implementation of the binding curricular requirements into school-specific requirements lies within the freedom of design – and duty of design – of the subject conferences as well as the pedagogical responsibility of the teachers. This creates the framework to specifically address and promote the competences and interests of the students or to enable additions by the respective school as a meaningful extension of the competences and content.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p12.translation: 12 2 Competence Areas, Content Fields, and Competence Expectations In the chapter "Tasks and Goals" of the core curricula, among other things, the goals of the subject as well as the general competences that students are to develop in the respective subject (cross-disciplinary subject competence) are described. They are differentiated by identifying and specifying subject-specific competence areas and content fields. This analytical approach is carried out in order to make the structuring of the subject-relevant processes on the one hand and the objects on the other hand transparent. Competence expectations link both sides together. This takes into account the fact that the simultaneous use of skills and knowledge plays a central role in mastering requirement situations. Competence areas represent the basic dimensions of subject-related action. They serve to structure the individual sub-operations along the subject-related processes and to clarify access for those involved in the teaching-learning process. Content fields systematize, with their respective content emphases, the binding and indispensable objects in teaching and provide indications for the content orientation of teaching and learning. Competence expectations bring processes and objects together and describe the subject-related requirements and intended learning outcomes. Goals of the subject/ Cross-disciplinary subject competence Chapter 1 Competence areas (processes) Chapter 2.1 Content fields (objects) Chapter 2.1 Competence expectations (linking processes and objects) Chapters 2.2, 2.3, and 2.4

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p13.translation: 13 Competency Expectations • refer to observable actions and are aimed at coping with challenging situations, • represent the expected knowledge, skills, and abilities at a medium level of abstraction in terms of standard rules, • describe results of cumulative, systematically interconnected learning, • can be implemented and verified in task formulations. Overall, instruction in lower secondary education is not limited solely to achieving the listed competency expectations but should enable students to further develop these and acquire additional knowledge and skills. The competency expectations and mandatory content described in the core curriculum for the end of lower secondary education are equally valid for the shortened (G8) as well as for the nine-year educational track (G9) of lower secondary education at the Gymnasium. The reduced instructional volume of the eight-year track is accounted for within the framework of the school-internal curriculum, among other things, by specifications regarding curricular progression and the type of didactic-methodical approach.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p14.translation: 14 2.1 Competence Areas and Content Fields of the Subject The development of the deepened mathematical basic education aimed for the subject of mathematics takes place through the conveyance of fundamental subject-specific processes, which can be assigned to the interrelated competence areas. Competence Areas Operating (Ope) Mathematical operating includes dealing with symbolic, formal, and technical elements of mathematics as well as switching between mathematical representations. Mathematical operating is expressed in a flexibly available ability to act, which can be used and justified situationally. It is a fundamental component of all mathematical processes. Operating without aids includes skills, routine tasks, and algorithmic procedures in the calculus area and is based on the sensible handling of mathematical objects. This enables the recognition of mathematical structures in novel situations and the application and further development of mathematical concepts. Working with media and tools also makes more complex matters accessible to mathematical processing and enables the visualization and dynamization of mathematical relationships. This facilitates making justified conjectures about universally valid statements and further processing them. A sensible handling of media and tools presupposes secure operating without aids. Modeling (Mod) To mathematically capture real situations and thus answer questions, the process of mathematical modeling is passed through in several partial steps. This process includes structuring the situation with regard to a question. On this, mathematization is based through mathematical concepts, structures, and relations; within the mathematical model, a solution is developed. For interpretation and validation, the solution must be understood as an answer to the qu

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p15.translation: 15 This process involves exploring the situation, based on that the purposeful solving, and reflecting on the found solution approaches. Arguing (Arg) In dealing with mathematical concepts and regularities, chains of argumentation are followed and further connections are suspected or discovered. Checking these and, if necessary, generalizing them is an essential part of mathematical arguing. Mathematical arguing includes making conjectures, justifying the recognized mathematical connections by referring to known facts and through the rules of mathematical reasoning and proving, as well as evaluating chains of argumentation. Communicating (Kom) Mathematical communicating involves the audience- and content-appropriate verbalization of mathematical facts, problem situations, and solution ideas. The use of technical language enables mathematical statements to be formulated precisely and unambiguously. For mathematics, in addition to verbal representation, iconic and symbolic representations are of central importance. Mathematical communicating includes the reception, production, and discussion of subject-specific treatments. Content areas Competencies are always tied to subject content. Therefore, the deepened mathematical basic education should be developed with regard to the following content areas by the end of lower secondary education. Arithmetic/Algebra (Ari) The extension of number sets from natural numbers up to real numbers and the generalization of the concrete handling of numbers through variables, terms, equations, and systems of equations are subjects of arithmetic and algebra. In fraction calculation, familiar basic concepts are expanded and numbers are identified with parts. The basic arithmetic operations are transferred to new number sets, generalized, and extended by exponentiation, root extraction, and logarithmization.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p16.translation: 16 Functions (Fkt) Assignments and functions allow the dependence of two quantities to be described and applied in quantitative contexts. Various forms of representation are used and transformed into each other appropriately to the situation. Starting from simple assignments, a precise concept of function is developed, on which new classes of functions are based and these themselves become objects of mathematical investigations. Functions are used as models for diverse application situations; their parameters and properties are accessible to interpretation. With the help of functions, a part of reality can thus be described quantitatively. Geometry (Geo) Geometric objects in plane and space can be described, classified, measured, and constructed. These objects are represented in various forms and transformed by mappings. Geometry is particularly suitable for making universally valid discoveries, building a structure of concepts and theorems, and conducting first proofs. Increasingly, formulas and theorems are used as analytical tools for processing geometric issues in mathematical and non-mathematical contexts. Stochastics (Sto) In many socially relevant areas, stochastic concepts, data, and probability statements play a central role. In stochastics, data are mathematically processed and represented as well as examined by determining relevant key figures. Based on a robust concept of probability, random phenomena in everyday situations can be interpreted. Starting from relative frequencies, statistical statements in authentic texts are assessed using stochastic theorems. Networking of content areas The content areas Arithmetic/Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Stochastics are not to be considered isolated side by side; rather, they are con

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p17.translation: 17 to identify both the commonalities and the particularities of the content areas and to use the underlying concepts flexibly. Linking competence areas and content areas In lower secondary education, subject-specific processes are established, consolidated, and made conscious. Through the connection with content areas in increasingly complex and cognitively demanding learning situations, process-related competences are deepened, differentiated, and networked with each other. In terms of expected mathematical competences, in principle, every link between subject-specific processes and subject-specific objects is conceivable and relevant. However, teaching does not have to explicitly consider every single link. Some of the links have a particularly high significance for doing mathematics and are therefore specified by this core curriculum.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p18.translation: 18 2.2 Process-related competency expectations by the end of lower secondary education In the five competency areas, the characteristic processes of the subject—operating, modeling, problem-solving, arguing, and communicating—are presented with binding competency expectations. By the end of lower secondary education, students should—building on the competency development in primary education—possess the process-related competencies named below regarding the mandatory content. In this chapter, overarching process-related competency expectations are first listed for all competency areas (processes), and in chapters 2.3 and 2.4, competency expectations are formulated in a content-field-related manner. Operating Operating without aids Students apply basic mental arithmetic skills confidently, (1) spatially imagine geometric situations and switch between (2) perspectives, translate symbolic and formal language into natural language and (3) vice versa, perform appropriate arithmetic operations based on a content-related (4) understanding, work with (5) variables, terms, equations, and functions considering mathematical rules and laws, confidently perform changes of representation, (6) carry out solution and control procedures safely and efficiently, (7) use schematized and strategy-guided procedures, algorithms, and (8) rules. Working with media and tools Students use mathematical aids (ruler, set square, and compass) for meas-(9) uring, precise drawing, and constructing,

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p19.translation: 19 use information and data from media offerings (print media, internet and formula collection) for information research, use digital mathematics tools (dynamic geometry software, function plotters, computer algebra systems, multi-representation systems, calculators and spreadsheets), decide appropriately for the situation about the use of mathematical aids and digital mathematics tools and select them with justification, use analog and digital media to support and design mathematical processes. Modeling Structuring The students capture real situations and describe them with words and sketches, (1) pose their own questions about real situations that can be answered using mathematical knowledge and skills, (2) make justified assumptions and simplify real situations. (3) Mathematical modeling The students translate real situations into mathematical models or select suitable models and use appropriate representations, assign suitable real situations to a mathematical model, (5) develop solutions using mathematical knowledge and skills (6) within the mathematical model. Interpreting and validating The students relate developed solutions to the real situation and interpret (7) them as answers to the question, check solutions for their plausibility in real situations, (8) name limits of established mathematical models and improve (9) established models with regard to the question.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p20.translation: 20 Problem Solving Exploring Students reproduce problem situations in their own words and ask questions about (1) a given problem situation, select suitable heuristic aids (sketch, informative figure, table, experimental methods), continue patterns and number sequences, describe relationships between (3) quantities and formulate justified conjectures about connections. Solving Students select appropriate concepts, relationships, methods, media and tools for problem solving, use heuristic strategies and principles (finding examples, finding special cases, analogy considerations, estimating and approximating, systematic trying or excluding, changing representations, decomposing and completing, using symmetries, finding invariants, reducing to known, decomposing into subproblems, case distinctions, forward and backward working, reasoning, generalizing), develop ideas for possible solution approaches, plan procedures for (6) solving a problem and carry out solution plans purposefully. Reflecting Students check the plausibility of results, (7) compare different solution methods with regard to similarities (8) and differences and assess their efficiency, analyze and reflect on causes of errors, (9) name underlying heuristic strategies and principles and (10) transfer these justifiedly to other problem situations.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p21.translation: 21 Arguing Suspecting Students ask questions that are characteristic for mathematics and formulate justified conjectures about the existence and nature of relationships, name examples of suspected relationships, specify conjectures using technical terms and taking into account the logical structure. Justifying Students establish relations between technical terms (superordinate/subordinate concept), justify solution methods and use mathematical rules or theorems and factual-logical arguments, link arguments into chains of reasoning, use different argumentation strategies (counterexample, direct inference, contradiction), explain given arguments and proofs with regard to their logical structure (implications/equivalence, and/or connections, negation, universal and existential statements). Evaluating Students assess whether given chains of reasoning are complete and error-free, supplement incomplete and correct faulty chains of reasoning. Communicating Receiving Students extract and structure information from mathematics-related texts and representations, research and evaluate subject-related information.

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p22.translation: 22 explain conceptual contents based on typical internal and external mathematical application situations. Producing The students reproduce observations, known solution methods and procedures in their own (4) words and with the help of mathematical terms, verbalize their own thought processes and describe their own solution methods, (5) use the subject-specific language to an appropriate extent, (6) choose suitable forms of representation depending on the situation and purpose, (7) document work steps comprehensibly and present them. (8) Discuss The students take up contributions and develop them further, (9) compare and assess elaborations and presentations with regard to (10) their technical correctness, comprehensibility and subject-specific language quality, make decisions on the basis of subject-related discussions (11).

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p23.translation: 23 2.3 Competency Expectations and Content Focuses up to the End of the Trial Stage At the end of the trial stage, students should – building on the competency development in primary school – possess the competencies regarding the mandatory content mentioned below. The competencies are to be developed within the framework of working on the following content areas mandatory for the grades up to the end of the trial stage: − Arithmetic/Algebra − Functions − Geometry − Stochastics If one links the mathematical processes and their overarching process-related competency expectations (Section 2.2) with the listed mandatory content areas, the following concretized competency expectations result. Arithmetic/Algebra Content Focuses: – Basic arithmetic operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of natural numbers, simple fractions, and finite decimal numbers, written division – Laws and rules: commutative, associative, and distributive laws for addition and multiplication of natural numbers, divisibility rules – Concept formation: prime factorization, shares, fractions of quantities, reducing, expanding, arithmetic expression – Number range extension: positive rational numbers, representation of integers – Representation: place value chart, number line, word form, fraction, finite and periodic decimal number, percentage – Quantities and units: length, area, volume, time, money, mass Students explain properties of prime numbers, decompose natural numbers into (1) prime factors and use exponent notation in doing so (Ope-4, Arg-4), determine divisors of natural numbers, apply divisibility rules (2) for 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 and combine these into further divisibility rules (Arg-5, Arg-6, Arg-7),

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p24.translation: 24 justify strategies for advantageous calculation using calculation laws and use them (Ope-4, Arg-5), verbalize calculation terms using technical terms and translate calculation instructions and real-life situations into calculation terms (Ope-3, Mod-4, Kom-6), reverse calculation instructions (Pro-6, Pro-7), (5) use variables in the description of simple real-life contexts and in the formulation of calculation laws (Ope-5, Mod-4, Mod-5), substitute numbers into terms with variables and calculate their value (7) (Ope-5, Mod-6), represent numbers in different ways, compare them and switch appropriately between the different representations (Ope-6, Kom-7), estimate quantities, select units of quantities appropriately for the situation and (9) convert them (Ope-7, Mod-3, Pro-5), round numbers meaningfully in context and apply approximation and checking as (10) control strategies (Ope-7, Mod-7, Mod-8), interpret fractions as parts, operators, quotients, numbers and ratios (11) (Pro-2, Arg-4, Kom-3), reduce and expand fractions and interpret this as coarsening or refining the division (Ope-4, Pro-2, Kom-5), calculate and interpret fraction, part and whole in context (Mod-4, (13) Pro-4, Kom-3), perform basic arithmetic operations in different representations both mentally (14) and in writing and present calculation steps comprehensibly (Ope-1, Kom-5, Kom-8), use integers to describe states and changes (15) in real-life contexts and as coordinates (Mod-1, Mod-4, Pro-5, Arg-2).

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p25.translation: 25 Functions Content Focus: – Relationship between quantities: diagram, table, verbal form, scale, rule of three The students describe the relationship between two quantities using words, diagrams, and tables (Mod-1, Mod-4, Com-1, Com-7), apply the rule of three to solve practical problems (Ope-8, Mod-3, Mod-6, Mod-8), explore patterns in number sequences and describe the regularities in words and with terms (Pro-1, Pro-3, Pro-5), calculate with scales and create drawings in appropriate scales (Ope-4, Ope-9). Geometry Content Focus: – Plane figures: circle, special triangles, special quadrilaterals, angles, segment, line, Cartesian coordinate system, drawing, perimeter and area (rectangle, right triangle), decomposition and completion strategies – Solids: cuboid, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere, oblique projections and nets (cuboid and cube), surface area and volume (cuboid and cube) – Positional relationships and symmetry: parallelism, orthogonality, point and axis symmetry – Transformations: translations, rotations, point and axis reflections The students explain basic concepts and use them to describe plane figures and solids as well as their positional relationships to each other (Ope-3, Com-3), characterize and classify special quadrilaterals (Arg-4, Arg-6, Com-6), identify and characterize solids in pictorial representations and in the environment (Ope-2, Mod-3, Mod-4, Com-3), draw plane figures using appropriate tools such as compass, ruler, and set square as well as dynamic geometry software (Ope-9, Ope-11, Ope-12),

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p26.translation: 26 generate plane symmetrical figures and patterns and determine axes of symmetry or points of symmetry (Ope-8, Pro-3, Pro-9), represent plane figures in the Cartesian coordinate system (Ope-9, Ope-11), generate mappings of plane figures by translation and reflection, also in the coordinate system (Ope-9, Ope-11, Pro-6), use dynamic geometry software to analyze compositions of mappings of plane figures (Ope-11, Ope-13), estimate and measure the size of angles and classify angles with technical terms (Ope-9, Kom-3, Kom-6), estimate the length of segments and determine them using scales (Pro-5, Arg-7), use the basic principle of measuring in determining area and volume (Pro-4, Arg-5), calculate the perimeter of quadrilaterals, the area of rectangles and right-angled triangles, as well as the surface area and volume of cuboids (Ope-4, Ope-8), determine the area of plane figures through decomposition and completion strategies (Arg-3, Arg-5), describe the result of rotations and translations of a cuboid from imagination (Ope-2, Kom-5), represent cuboids and cubes as nets, oblique drawings, and models and recognize solids from their corresponding representations (Ope-2, Mod-1, Kom-3). Stochastics Content focal points: – statistical data: data collection, tally and stroke lists, class division, bar and pie charts, boxplots – concept formation: relative and absolute frequency – characteristic values: arithmetic mean, median, range, quartiles The students collect data, summarize it in tally and stroke lists and form suitable class divisions (Mod-3, Kom-2),

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p27.translation: 27 represent frequencies in tables and diagrams also using digital mathematical tools (spreadsheet) (Ope-11), determine, compare and interpret frequencies and characteristic values of statistical data (Mod-7, Arg-1, Kom-1), read and interpret graphical representations of statistical surveys (Mod-2, Kom-1, Kom-2), attribute changes in statistical characteristic values to the influence of individual data points of a data set (Ope-4, Arg-2, Arg-3), discuss advantages and disadvantages of graphical representations (Mod-8, Arg-9).

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p28.translation: 28 2.4 Competency Expectations and Content Focuses up to the End of Lower Secondary Education At the end of lower secondary education, students should possess the competencies regarding the mandatory content listed below. The competencies are to be developed within the framework of working on the following content fields mandatory for the grade levels up to the end of lower secondary education: − Arithmetic/Algebra − Functions − Geometry − Stochastics If one links the mathematical processes and their overarching process-related competency expectations (Section 2.2) with the listed mandatory content fields, the following concretized competency expectations result. 2.4.1 First Stage Arithmetic/Algebra Content Focuses: – Number range extension: rational numbers – Term and variable: variable as a variable quantity, as a placeholder, and as an unknown, term transformations – Laws and rules: sign rules, calculation laws for rational numbers, binomial formulas – Solution methods: algebraic and graphical solution methods (linear equations and linear systems of equations with two variables, elementary fractional equations) Students represent rational numbers on the number line and order them by size (Ope-6, Pro-3), give reasons and examples for number range extensions (Mod-3, Arg-7), derive sign rules for addition and multiplication based on examples and use calculation laws and rules (Ope-8, Arg-5),

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p29.translation: 29 interpret variables as variables for describing mappings, as (4) placeholders in terms and calculation rules as well as unknowns in equations and systems of equations (Mod-4, Mod-5, Pro-4), represent terms as calculation rules of mappings and for the calculation (5) of areas and volumes (Mod-4, Mod-6, Kom-1), set up equations and inequalities to formulate conditions (6) in real-world situations (Mod-3, Mod-9), transform terms, including fractional terms, purposefully and correct faulty (7) term transformations (Ope-5, Pro-9), determine exponents in the context of interest calculation by systematic (8) trial also using spreadsheet calculations (Pro-4, Pro-5, Ope-11), determine solution sets of linear equations and linear systems of equations as well as fractional equations using appropriate methods and interpret them in the real-world context (Ope-8, Mod-7, Pro-6), select algebraic solution methods for linear systems of equations purposefully (10) and compare the efficiency of different solution methods (Pro-4, Pro-8, Pro-10). Functions Content focal points: – proportional and inversely proportional mapping: mapping rule, graph, table, verbal form, quotient equality, proportionality factor, product equality, rule of three – linear functions: function term, graph, table, verbal form, axis intercepts, slope, slope triangle – percentage and interest calculation: base value, percentage value, percentage rate, percentage change, growth factor The students characterize mappings and distinguish them from each other based on their properties (1) (Arg-3, Arg-4, Kom-1), describe real-world situations matching given mappings (2) (Mod-5, Kom-3), characterize functions as a class of unique mappings (Arg-4, (3) Kom-3),

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p30.translation: 30 represent functions in their own words, in value tables, as graphs, and as terms (4) and use the representations appropriately to the situation (Kom-4, Kom-6, Kom-7), describe the influence of parameters on the graph of a linear (5) function using technical terms (Arg-1, Arg-3, Arg-7), interpret the parameters of a linear function term taking into account (6) the units in real-world situations (Mod-8, Arg-5), solve purely mathematical and everyday problems using mappings and functions also with digital mathematical tools (calculators, spreadsheets, function plotters, and multi-representation systems) (Ope-11, Mod-6, Pro-6), apply percentage and interest calculations to general consumption situations (8) and create application-related spreadsheets with relative and absolute cell references (Ope-11, Ope-13, Mod-2), describe percentage changes with growth factors and combine percentage changes (Mod-4, Pro-3). nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p32.translation: 32 2.4.2 Second Level Arithmetic/Algebra Content Focus: – Extension of number range: real numbers – Concept formation: powers, roots, logarithms – Laws and rules: laws of exponents, laws of roots – Solution methods and algorithms: algorithmic approximation methods, solution methods for quadratic equations (completing the square, p-q formula, Vieta's theorem), solution methods for exponential equations of the form xbc = (systematic trial, logarithmizing) The students represent numbers in decimal exponent notation (Ope-1, Ope-6), (1) distinguish rational and irrational numbers and give examples of irrational numbers (Arg-2, Com-3), simplify terms in which the laws of exponents are directly applicable (Ope-5, Com-7), (3) switch between fractional representation and exponent notation (Ope-1, (4) Ope-6), switch between root and exponent notation (Ope-1, Ope-6), (5) use and describe an algorithmic procedure to approximate square roots (Ope-8, Pro-5, Com-4), (6) calculate square roots using the laws of roots also without digital (7) tools (Ope-1, Ope-5), select methods for solving quadratic equations with justification, (8) compare their efficiency and determine the solution set of a quadratic equation also without aids (Pro-4, Pro-8, Ope-7), apply root extraction as the inverse of exponentiation (Ope-4), (9) solve exponential equations xbc = approximately by trial, (10) by logarithmizing as well as with digital mathematical tools (Pro-5, Ope-12), apply their knowledge of quadratic equations and exponential (11) equations to solve intra- and extra-mathematical problems and interpret results in contexts (Mod-7, Mod-8, Mod-9, Pro-4).

Stochastics Content focus: – statistical data: collection, diagram, manipulation – probabilities and random experiments: conditional probability, stochastic independence, four-field table, tree diagrams, path rules The students plan statistical data collections and use digital tools for recording and evaluation (Ope-11, Kom-8), critically analyze graphical representations of statistical surveys and recognize manipulations (Arg-9, Kom-10, Kom-11), use two-stage random experiments to represent random occurrences in everyday situations (Mod-4), carry out combinatorial considerations in concrete situations to determine the number of respective possibilities (Pro-4, Pro-5, Pro-7), calculate probabilities using tree diagrams and four-field tables and interpret these in the context of the situation (Ope-8, Mod-7, Mod-8), interpret and assess data and statistical statements in authentic texts (Mod-7, Mod-8, Arg-9, Kom-10, Kom-11).

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p36.translation: 36 3 Assessment of Learning Success and Performance Evaluation The legally binding principles of performance evaluation are set out in the School Act (§ 48 SchulG) as well as in the training and examination regulations for secondary level I (§ 6 APO-SI). Accordingly, in the performance evaluation of students in the subject of mathematics, achievements in the assessment areas "Written Work" as well as "Other Performance in Class" must be taken into account. The overall performance evaluation refers to the competencies acquired in connection with the instruction and presupposes that the students have had sufficient opportunity to acquire the competencies specified in Chapter 2. Successful learning is cumulative. This requires that instruction and assessments of learning success must be designed to give students the opportunity to repeatedly demonstrate competencies in varying contexts. For teachers, the results of the assessments of learning success are an occasion to review and, if necessary, modify the objectives and methods of their instruction. For students, feedback accompanying the learning process as well as reports on the achieved learning status should serve as an aid for self-assessment and an encouragement for further learning. This can also take place in phases of instruction in which no performance evaluation is conducted. The assessment of performance should also, in principle, be linked with the diagnosis of the achieved learning status and indications of individual learning progress. The performance evaluation is to be designed so that it corresponds to the principles decided in the subject conferences in accordance with the School Act (§ 70 para. 4 SchulG), that the criteria for grading are transparent to the students, and that the corrections as well as the comments also provide the learners with insights

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p37.translation: 37 Exercises during the course of lower secondary education prepare the students for the requirements of subsequent school and vocational training. Assessment area "Written work" Written work serves the written verification of competencies. They are to be designed so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge as well as their skills and abilities. They require appropriate preparation and demand clearly understandable task formulations. Taken as a whole, the task formulations should reflect the diversity of competencies and working methods acquired in lessons. Forms of assessment used for written work must be applied sufficiently and in a timely manner on various occasions so that students are familiar with them. For use in written work, forms of assessment – if necessary also in combination – can be considered that are listed in the last section of this chapter. To create appropriate transparency, the evaluation of written work is criteria-based. Once a school year, according to APO SI, a written work can be replaced by another, usually written, in exceptional cases also equivalent non-written performance assessment. In mathematics lessons, problems are deliberately worked on with or without aids (cf. Chapter 2.2). This should be taken into account in the written work. In the work, attention must be paid to a formally and subject-specifically correct presentation of the solution methods. Assessment area "Other performance in class" The assessment area "Other performance in class" captures the competence development of students recognizable in the teaching process through oral, written, and practical contributions. In the evaluation, the quality, the quantity and the con

nrw_g9_gymnasium_m_klp.pdf::p38.translation: 38 taken, but productively used for individual and general learning progress. The assessment area "Other achievements in class" – possibly also based on extracurricular preparation and follow-up of lessons – includes, among others: • contributions to class discussions, • appropriate and reflective use of analog and digital tools, • cooperative achievements within group work, • performance assessments required in class as well as • short written exercises. Possible forms of assessment The competency expectations of the core curriculum allow for a variety of forms of assessment. Throughout lower secondary education, as broad a spectrum as possible of the following forms of assessment should be used in written, oral, or practical contexts. In addition, other forms of assessment may be used at the teacher's discretion. In principle, all competency areas listed in Chapter 2 of the curriculum "Operating," "Modeling," "Problem Solving," "Arguing," and "Communicating" in connection with the respective content areas "Arithmetic/Algebra," "Functions," "Geometry," and "Stochastics" must be appropriately considered in performance evaluation. The following describes possible forms of assessment that appropriately consider both the process-related competency expectations and the concretized content-related competency expectations. These are suitable for use in class as learning tasks as well as forms of assessment. Combinations of different forms are also possible. The following list is not exhaustive.
